description: FitBot general-guidance knowledge base used for retrieval. Passages were written for this project to agree with the cited public-health sources. They contain no exact food nutrient values (those come only from USDA data).

sources.PAG: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition (2018).
sources.DGA: U.S. Department of Agriculture & HHS. Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025.
sources.CDC_SLEEP: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention - sleep duration recommendations (based on AASM/SRS consensus).
sources.ACSM_NUTR: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. Nutrition and Athletic Performance. ACSM / Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics / Dietitians of Canada joint position (2016).
sources.ISSN_PROTEIN: Jager R. et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: Protein and Exercise (2017).
sources.NASEM_WATER: National Academies. Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride and Sulfate (2004).
sources.FDA_CAFFEINE: U.S. Food and Drug Administration - Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine Is Too Much? (consumer update).
sources.CDC_WEIGHT: U.S. CDC - Losing Weight / Healthy Weight guidance.
sources.ACSM_GUIDE: American College of Sports Medicine - general exercise prescription guidance (FITT principle, warm-up, flexibility).

passages.title: Weekly activity guideline for adults
passages.text: Adults should aim for at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent mix. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups are recommended on 2 or more days per week. Some activity is better than none, and benefits increase with more activity.

passages.title: Sitting less
passages.text: Moving more and sitting less benefits nearly everyone. Breaking up long periods of sitting with short walks, stairs or light activity is helpful, especially for people who are just starting to exercise.

passages.title: Activity for children and teens
passages.text: Children and adolescents aged 6 to 17 should do 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, including vigorous activity, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week each.

passages.title: Activity for older adults
passages.text: Older adults should follow the adult guidelines as their abilities allow and include balance training as part of a multicomponent program. Those with chronic conditions should talk with a health professional about the types and amounts of activity that are appropriate for them.

passages.title: Judging cardio intensity
passages.text: A simple way to judge intensity is the talk test. During moderate-intensity activity such as brisk walking you can talk but not sing. During vigorous activity such as running you can only say a few words without pausing for breath.

passages.title: Benefits of cardio
passages.text: Regular aerobic activity improves heart and lung fitness, helps with weight management, improves mood and sleep, and lowers the risk of many chronic diseases. Walking, cycling, swimming, rowing, running and dancing all count.

passages.title: Starting cardio as a beginner
passages.text: Beginners can start with 10 to 20 minutes of brisk walking or easy cycling on most days and add a few minutes each week. Increasing duration first and intensity later lowers the risk of injury. Walk-run intervals are a good bridge to continuous running.

passages.title: HIIT vs steady-state cardio
passages.text: High-intensity interval training alternates short hard efforts with recovery and is time-efficient. Steady-state cardio at a moderate pace is easier to recover from and suits beginners. Both improve fitness; a mix works well, and HIIT is usually limited to 1 to 3 sessions per week.

passages.title: Building endurance
passages.text: Endurance improves by gradually increasing the total time or distance of aerobic training. A common rule of thumb is to increase weekly running volume by no more than about 10 percent, and to keep most sessions at an easy, conversational pace.

passages.title: Strength training basics
passages.text: Strength training should work all major muscle groups - legs, hips, back, chest, shoulders, arms and core - on at least 2 days per week. A set of 8 to 12 repetitions to near-fatigue is effective for most people, and 1 to 3 sets per exercise is a good start.

passages.title: How muscle growth works
passages.text: Muscle grows when resistance training challenges the muscles and the body has enough protein and energy to repair and build tissue. Progressive overload - gradually adding weight, reps or sets over time - is the key driver. Most people train each muscle group about twice a week with roughly 10 or more hard sets per week.

passages.title: Rep ranges for different goals
passages.text: Heavier loads for about 1 to 6 reps emphasise maximal strength, moderate loads for about 6 to 12 reps are popular for muscle growth, and lighter loads for 15 or more reps build muscular endurance. Muscle can grow across a wide range of reps when sets are taken close to fatigue.

passages.title: Rest between sets
passages.text: Rest about 2 to 3 minutes between sets of heavy compound lifts, about 1 to 2 minutes for moderate muscle-building sets, and 30 to 60 seconds for light or circuit-style work.

passages.title: Progressive overload
passages.text: Progressive overload means gradually increasing the challenge: a little more weight, an extra rep, an extra set, or better control. When you can complete the top of your rep range with good form for all sets, increase the weight slightly.

passages.title: Beginner program structure
passages.text: Beginners do well with 2 to 3 full-body sessions per week on non-consecutive days, using a few basic movements: a squat, a hinge, a push, a pull and a core exercise. Start with light weights, learn technique, and add load gradually.

passages.title: Training splits
passages.text: Full-body workouts 3 times per week suit beginners. Upper/lower splits 4 days per week and push/pull/legs splits suit intermediates who want more volume. The best split is the one you can follow consistently while recovering well.

passages.title: Training at home
passages.text: Effective workouts can be done at home with bodyweight exercises such as squats, lunges, push-ups, glute bridges and planks. Adding dumbbells, kettlebells or resistance bands allows more progression. Increase difficulty with more reps, slower tempo, harder variations or added weight.

passages.title: Dumbbell-only training
passages.text: A pair of dumbbells covers every major movement: goblet squats and lunges for legs, Romanian deadlifts for the hips and hamstrings, dumbbell presses and floor presses for the chest, rows for the back, shoulder presses and lateral raises for shoulders, and curls and extensions for the arms.

passages.title: First time in the gym
passages.text: Machines such as the leg press, lat pulldown, seated row and chest press are beginner-friendly because they guide the movement. Free weights add balance and coordination demands. Ask gym staff to show machine set-up, and start light.

passages.title: Warming up
passages.text: A warm-up of 5 to 10 minutes of light cardio and dynamic movements such as leg swings, arm circles and bodyweight squats raises body temperature and prepares joints. Before lifting, do one or two lighter sets of your first exercise.

passages.title: Cooling down
passages.text: A cool-down of about 5 to 10 minutes of easy movement lets your heart rate return gradually. It is a good time for static stretching while the muscles are warm.

passages.title: Static stretching guidance
passages.text: For flexibility, stretch major muscle groups at least 2 to 3 days per week, holding each static stretch for about 10 to 30 seconds to the point of mild tension, not pain, and repeating 2 to 4 times. Do not bounce.

passages.title: Dynamic vs static stretching
passages.text: Dynamic stretches move joints through their range of motion and are best before exercise. Long static stretches are better after a workout or as a separate flexibility session, because very long static holds right before explosive or heavy efforts may slightly reduce performance.

passages.title: Stretching for desk workers
passages.text: People who sit a lot often benefit from hip flexor stretches, chest and shoulder stretches, cat-cow spinal mobility and regular movement breaks every 30 to 60 minutes.

passages.title: How much sleep adults need
passages.text: Adults aged 18 to 60 need 7 or more hours of sleep per night. Teenagers need about 8 to 10 hours. Regularly sleeping less can impair recovery, performance, appetite control and mood.

passages.title: Sleep habits
passages.text: Helpful sleep habits include keeping a consistent sleep and wake time, a dark, quiet and cool bedroom, limiting screens before bed, avoiding large meals and alcohol close to bedtime, and avoiding caffeine late in the day.

passages.title: Sleep and training
passages.text: Sleep is when much of the body's recovery and adaptation happens. Short sleep is linked to lower training performance, higher perceived effort, and stronger hunger signals, which can make weight management harder.

passages.title: Exercise timing and sleep
passages.text: Regular physical activity generally helps people fall asleep and sleep more deeply. If intense evening workouts make it hard to fall asleep, finish them a couple of hours before bed or move them earlier.

passages.title: When to get help with sleep
passages.text: Ongoing insomnia, loud snoring with gasping, or excessive daytime sleepiness can signal a sleep disorder and should be discussed with a doctor.

passages.title: Rest days
passages.text: Muscles adapt between sessions, not during them. Most people benefit from at least 1 to 2 rest days per week and about 48 hours before training the same muscle group hard again. Light walking or mobility work on rest days (active recovery) is fine.

passages.title: Muscle soreness (DOMS)
passages.text: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after new or harder exercise and fades on its own. Gentle movement, sleep, hydration and adequate protein help. Sharp pain, swelling, or pain that does not improve is different from soreness and should be checked by a professional.

passages.title: Signs of overtraining
passages.text: Persistent fatigue, falling performance, poor sleep, irritability, frequent illness and lingering soreness can mean training load is higher than recovery allows. Reducing volume or taking a lighter week (a deload) usually helps.

passages.title: Nutrition for recovery
passages.text: Recovery is supported by enough total energy, protein spread across the day, carbohydrates to refill glycogen after hard or long sessions, fluids to replace sweat losses, and good sleep.

passages.title: Protein needs
passages.text: The general adult RDA for protein is 0.8 g per kg of body weight per day. People who exercise regularly, especially those trying to build muscle, are commonly advised 1.2 to 2.0 g per kg per day, spread over meals with roughly 20 to 40 g of protein each.

passages.title: Protein sources
passages.text: Good protein sources include eggs, poultry, fish, lean meat, Greek yogurt, milk, cottage cheese, tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans, chickpeas, edamame, nuts and seeds. Plant proteins can fully meet needs when a variety is eaten across the day.

passages.title: Vegetarian and vegan protein
passages.text: Vegetarians can get protein from dairy, eggs, tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans, chickpeas, edamame, soy milk, nuts and seeds. Vegans can rely on soy foods, legumes, seitan, nuts and seeds, and may need to plan vitamin B12, iron, calcium and omega-3 intake.

passages.title: Carbohydrates and exercise
passages.text: Carbohydrates are the main fuel for moderate and high-intensity exercise. Whole grains, fruit, vegetables, potatoes and legumes provide carbohydrates plus fiber and micronutrients. Rice, pasta and bread are fine in a fitness diet; portion size and overall balance matter more than avoiding any single food.

passages.title: Dietary fat
passages.text: Fat is essential for hormones and absorbing vitamins A, D, E and K. Unsaturated fats from olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado and fatty fish are preferred, while saturated fat should be kept below 10 percent of daily calories.

passages.title: Fiber
passages.text: Fiber supports digestion and fullness. A common target is about 14 g of fiber per 1,000 calories eaten. Beans, lentils, whole grains, oats, vegetables, fruit, nuts and seeds are good sources.

passages.title: Energy balance
passages.text: Body weight changes when calories eaten differ from calories used over time. A modest calorie deficit leads to weight loss, a surplus leads to weight gain. Individual calorie needs vary with age, size, sex and activity level.

passages.title: Safe rate of weight loss
passages.text: Gradual weight loss of about 0.5 to 1 kg (1 to 2 pounds) per week is more likely to be maintained. Crash diets, very low calorie intakes and skipping meals are hard to sustain and can lead to muscle loss and nutrient shortfalls.

passages.title: Weight loss habits
passages.text: Helpful habits for fat loss include eating mostly minimally processed foods, filling half the plate with vegetables and fruit, including protein at each meal, limiting sugary drinks, watching portion sizes, staying active, sleeping enough and tracking progress.

passages.title: Exercise for weight loss
passages.text: Combining aerobic activity with strength training supports fat loss while helping preserve muscle. Many people need more than 150 minutes per week of moderate activity to lose weight and keep it off. Diet changes usually have the bigger effect on the calorie deficit.

passages.title: Spot reduction myth
passages.text: You cannot choose where your body loses fat. Crunches strengthen the abs but do not specifically burn belly fat. Overall fat loss through diet, activity and sleep reduces fat everywhere over time.

passages.title: Eating to build muscle
passages.text: To build muscle, combine progressive resistance training with enough protein (about 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg per day is often used) and a small calorie surplus. A slower gain helps limit fat gain. Beginners can often build muscle while losing some fat.

passages.title: Pre-workout eating
passages.text: A meal with carbohydrates and some protein 1 to 3 hours before training helps fuel performance - for example oats with milk and fruit, or rice with chicken. If you train soon after eating, choose a small, easily digested snack such as a banana or yogurt.

passages.title: Post-workout eating
passages.text: After training, a meal or snack with about 20 to 40 g of protein plus carbohydrates supports muscle repair and refuels glycogen - for example chicken with rice and vegetables, Greek yogurt with fruit, eggs on whole-wheat toast, a tofu stir-fry, or a milk-based smoothie. Eating within a few hours is sufficient for most people.

passages.title: Healthy breakfast ideas
passages.text: A balanced breakfast combines protein, fiber-rich carbohydrates and some fruit or vegetables - for example oats with milk or yogurt and berries, eggs with whole-wheat toast and tomatoes, or Greek yogurt with fruit and nuts.

passages.title: Healthy snack ideas
passages.text: Snacks that combine protein or fiber keep you fuller: Greek yogurt, fruit with a handful of nuts, hummus with vegetables, a boiled egg, cottage cheese, edamame, or air-popped popcorn.

passages.title: Foods and drinks to limit
passages.text: The Dietary Guidelines recommend keeping added sugars below 10 percent of daily calories, saturated fat below 10 percent, and sodium below 2,300 mg per day for most adults. Foods often worth limiting include sugary drinks, sweets, pastries, deep-fried foods and highly processed snacks. No single food is forbidden; frequency and portion size matter.

passages.title: Sugary drinks
passages.text: Sugar-sweetened beverages such as regular soda, energy drinks, sweetened teas and fruit drinks are among the largest sources of added sugar and are easy to over-consume because liquid calories do not fill you up. Water, unsweetened tea or coffee, and milk are better everyday choices.

passages.title: Alcohol and fitness
passages.text: Alcohol adds calories, can disturb sleep and may impair recovery. Adults who drink are advised to limit intake to 2 drinks or fewer per day for men and 1 or fewer for women, and drinking less is better for health.

passages.title: Daily water needs
passages.text: The National Academies set adequate total water intake at about 3.7 litres per day for men and 2.7 litres for women, including water from food and all beverages. Needs rise with heat, sweating and activity. Pale yellow urine is a simple sign of good hydration.

passages.title: Hydration during exercise
passages.text: Drink fluids before, during and after exercise, especially in heat. For most workouts under an hour, water is enough. For long or very sweaty sessions, fluids with electrolytes and carbohydrates can help. Drinking excessive amounts of plain water during very long events can be dangerous, so drink to thirst rather than forcing fluids.

passages.title: Electrolytes
passages.text: Sweat contains sodium and smaller amounts of potassium. Regular meals usually replace these for typical workouts. Sports drinks or electrolyte tablets are mainly useful for long-duration exercise, heavy sweating or hot conditions.

passages.title: Caffeine
passages.text: For healthy adults, the FDA notes up to about 400 mg of caffeine per day is generally not associated with negative effects. Caffeine can modestly improve exercise performance, but it can disturb sleep if taken late in the day. Pregnant people, people with heart conditions, and those sensitive to caffeine should check with a health professional.

passages.title: Supplements
passages.text: Most people can meet their needs with food. Protein powder is a convenient food, not a requirement. Creatine monohydrate is one of the most researched supplements for strength training. Supplements are not tightly regulated, so choose third-party tested products and avoid products promising rapid fat loss or muscle gain. Ask a doctor or pharmacist if you have a medical condition or take medication.

passages.title: Building a balanced plate
passages.text: A practical balanced plate is about half vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein foods and a quarter whole grains or starchy foods, plus a source of healthy fat and a glass of water or milk.

passages.title: Rice in a fitness diet
passages.text: Rice is a good carbohydrate source for active people and fits well into a fitness diet. Brown rice has more fiber than white rice, while white rice is easy to digest around training. Pair rice with protein and vegetables and match the portion to your energy needs.

passages.title: Eggs
passages.text: Eggs are an affordable source of high-quality protein along with vitamins and minerals, and they fit well in breakfasts and post-workout meals.

passages.title: Lifting safely
passages.text: Learn correct technique with light weights before adding load, warm up, control the weight through the whole movement, use spotters or safety bars for heavy pressing and squatting, and stop if you feel sharp pain. Progress gradually.

passages.title: Pain vs normal effort
passages.text: Muscle burning during a set and mild next-day soreness are normal. Sharp, stabbing or joint pain, pain that changes how you move, numbness, or pain that persists for days are warning signs - stop the exercise and consult a healthcare professional or physiotherapist.

passages.title: Stop exercising and seek help
passages.text: Stop exercising immediately and seek medical help for chest pain or pressure, severe shortness of breath, fainting or dizziness, an irregular heartbeat, or sudden severe headache.

passages.title: Checking with a doctor
passages.text: People with heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, recent surgery, pregnancy complications or other chronic conditions should talk with a healthcare provider before starting a new vigorous exercise program.

passages.title: Exercising in heat
passages.text: In hot weather, exercise during cooler parts of the day, wear light clothing, drink fluids regularly and reduce intensity. Dizziness, confusion, nausea or stopping sweating can signal heat illness and need immediate attention.

passages.title: Choosing dumbbells
passages.text: Adjustable dumbbells save space and allow progression. Beginners often start with a light pair for shoulders and arms and a heavier pair for legs, back and chest. Choose a weight you can lift for the target reps with good form, leaving 1 to 3 reps in reserve.

passages.title: Resistance bands
passages.text: Resistance bands are cheap, portable and joint-friendly. They work for rows, presses, squats, glute work and mobility, and are great for travel or home training. Check bands for tears before use.

passages.title: Simple home gym
passages.text: A simple home setup can include adjustable dumbbells, a sturdy bench, resistance bands, a pull-up bar and an exercise mat. A jump rope adds inexpensive cardio.

passages.title: Training shoes
passages.text: Running shoes are cushioned for repetitive impact. For lifting, flat stable shoes help balance. Replace running shoes when the cushioning is worn out.

passages.title: Consistency and habits
passages.text: Consistency matters more than perfection. Choose activities you enjoy, schedule workouts like appointments, set small specific goals, track progress, and expect motivation to vary - routines and habits carry you through.

passages.title: Exercise and stress
passages.text: Regular physical activity can reduce feelings of anxiety and improve mood. Walking outdoors, yoga, and moderate exercise are good options when stressed. Persistent low mood or anxiety should be discussed with a healthcare professional.

passages.title: Healthy lifestyle pillars
passages.text: A healthy lifestyle combines regular activity, balanced nutrition, adequate sleep, stress management, limited alcohol, no smoking, and staying socially connected.

passages.title: Beginner, intermediate and advanced
passages.text: Beginners (under about 6 months of consistent training) progress quickly with simple full-body plans. Intermediates usually need more volume and structured progression. Advanced lifters progress slowly and benefit from periodised programs and careful recovery management.

passages.title: Core training
passages.text: The core includes the abdominals, obliques, lower back and hip muscles. Planks, dead bugs, leg raises and rotation-control exercises build stability. Compound lifts such as squats and deadlifts also train the core.

passages.title: Disordered eating
passages.text: Severely restricting food, skipping meals to compensate for eating, purging, or excessive exercise to make up for food are signs of disordered eating. These need support from a doctor, registered dietitian or mental health professional.

passages.title: Exercise during pregnancy
passages.text: Healthy pregnant and postpartum people are generally encouraged to do at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week, but exercise plans during pregnancy should be discussed with an obstetric healthcare provider, especially with complications.
